content: The implant is a highly effective contraceptive method, with studies indicating its efficacy for up to five years. It has replaced the earlier version, Implanon, with the newer Implanon NXT, which is visible on X-rays and features an improved insertion device. The implant primarily works by preventing ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries) and by thickening cervical mucus, which blocks sperm from reaching an egg. Effectiveness: The implant is one of the most effective and long-lasting contraceptive methods available. During the first year of use, fewer than 1 pregnancy occurs per 1,000 women using the implant, meaning 999 out of 1,000 women will not become pregnant. Over the entire duration of use, the risk of pregnancy remains extremely low, though a small risk persists beyond the first year. Heavier women may experience a slight reduction in effectiveness near the end of the labeled duration of use (e.g., 5 years for Jadelle or 4 years for Levoplant) and may consider replacing the implant earlier. Fertility and STI Protection: Fertility returns immediately after the implant is removed, with no delay. The implant does not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Suitability: The implant is safe and effective for nearly all women, including those who: Have or have not had children. Are married or unmarried. Are of any age, including adolescents and women over 40. Have recently had an abortion, miscarriage, or ectopic pregnancy. Smoke cigarettes, regardless of age or smoking frequency. Are breastfeeding. Have anemia (current or past). Have varicose veins. Are living with HIV, whether or not they are on antiretroviral therapy. Insertion and Removal: The implant must be inserted by a trained healthcare provider. It is crucial to remove the implant before it loses effectiveness. Women can choose to have a new implant inserted if desired. Common Side Effects: Changes in bleeding patterns are common, especially during the first few months to a year. These may include: Lighter bleeding and fewer days of bleeding. Prolonged bleeding. Irregular bleeding. Infrequent bleeding. No monthly bleeding. After about one year, bleeding patterns may stabilize, with many women experiencing lighter or no monthly bleeding. Other reported side effects include: Headaches. Abdominal pain. Acne (which may improve or worsen). Weight changes. Breast tenderness. Dizziness. Mood changes. Nausea. Enlarged ovarian follicles (rare). Health Benefits: The implant helps protect against: Risks associated with pregnancy, including ectopic pregnancy. Symptomatic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). It may also reduce the risk of iron-deficiency anemia and ectopic pregnancy. Health Risks: No known health risks are associated with the implant. Counseling on Side Effects: Side effects are not indicative of illness, and the absence of bleeding does not mean pregnancy. Most side effects diminish or resolve within the first year of use. While side effects are common, some women may not experience any. Women should feel encouraged to return for assistance if side effects are bothersome or if they have other concerns. Special Considerations: Women with certain medical conditions should generally avoid using implants. However, in special circumstances where other methods are unavailable or unacceptable, a qualified provider may assess the woman’s condition and determine if implant use is appropriate. Conditions requiring careful consideration include: Acute blood clots in the legs or lungs. Unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation for serious underlying conditions. A history of breast cancer more than five years ago, with no recurrence. Severe liver cirrhosis or liver tumors. Systemic lupus erythematosus with positive or unknown antiphospholipid antibodies, especially if not on immunosuppressive therapy. Follow-Up for Continuing Users: Routine follow-up visits are not required until it is time to remove the implant. However, women should be encouraged to return at any time if they have questions or concerns. During follow-up visits, providers should: 1. Ask how the woman is doing with the method and if she is satisfied. 2. Address any concerns about bleeding changes and provide necessary information or support. 3. Inquire about any new health problems since the last visit and address them as needed. 4. Discuss major life changes, such as plans for children or STI/HIV risk, and provide appropriate guidance. 5. If the woman wishes to continue using the implant and no new medical conditions prevent its use, remind her of how much longer the implant will remain effective. DMPA Injectable Contraceptive: DMPA (Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate) is a progestin-only injectable contraceptive administered intramuscularly. It does not contain estrogen, making it suitable for breastfeeding women (starting six weeks postpartum) and those who cannot use estrogen-containing methods. The injection works primarily by preventing ovulation. Effectiveness: Effectiveness depends on receiving injections on time. Missing an injection increases the risk of pregnancy. When used correctly, fewer than 1 pregnancy occurs per 100 women in the first year of use. With typical use, about 4 pregnancies occur per 100 women in the first year. Fertility typically returns about four months after stopping DMPA, which is longer than most other methods. Side Effects: Most users experience changes in monthly bleeding, including: Irregular or prolonged bleeding during the first three months. No monthly bleeding, infrequent bleeding, or irregular bleeding after one year. Other reported side effects include: Weight gain (1–2 kg per year). Headaches. Dizziness. Abdominal bloating and discomfort. Mood changes. Reduced sex drive. Loss of bone density (potentially reversible). Health Benefits: DMPA helps protect against: Risks of pregnancy. Endometrial cancer. Uterine fibroids. It may also reduce: Symptomatic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Iron-deficiency anemia. Sickle cell crises in women with sickle cell anemia. Symptoms of endometriosis, such as pelvic pain and irregular bleeding. Counseling on Side Effects: Side effects are not signs of illness. While side effects are common, some women may not experience them. Women should feel encouraged to return for help if side effects are bothersome. Special Considerations: Women with certain conditions should generally avoid DMPA. However, in special circumstances, a qualified provider may assess the woman’s condition and determine if DMPA is appropriate. Conditions requiring careful consideration include: Breastfeeding within six weeks postpartum. Severe high blood pressure (≥160/100 mmHg). Acute blood clots in the legs or lungs. A history of heart disease.
